name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,672

clue.text: Some home 'so' carpeted in tasteful bit of peach?

indicators.note: 'some' asks for only part of what follows, so the letters sit inside a longer run of words

blocks.note: the run of letters straddles the three words, ignoring spaces and quotation marks

explanation.surface: A homely description of a peach so tasteful it might be wall-to-wall carpeted.
explanation.walkthrough: Read through hoMESOCARPeted: the quoted 'so' only exists to bridge the gap. The question mark flags that the definition is a little playful.
explanation.definitionFit: Botanists call the fleshy middle layer of a fruit's wall the mesocarp, which in a peach is the juicy part people eat.

clue.text: Vehicles in Perth you briefly examine

indicators.note: doing something briefly cuts it short, so the final letter is lopped off

blocks.note: U is text-speak for you
to examine is to test; cut short it loses its last letter

explanation.surface: Someone in Western Australia is invited to have a quick look over some cars.
explanation.walkthrough: Perth here is the city in Western Australia, which tells you an Australian word is wanted; a ute is short for utility vehicle.
explanation.definitionFit: Australians call a light pickup truck with an open tray a ute, so these are vehicles typical of any Perth street.

clue.text: Extremely hot organist needs to get jiggy

indicators.note: getting jiggy means dancing about wildly, so the letters are thrown into new positions

blocks.note: taken as written for rearranging

explanation.surface: A sexy church musician is in the mood to let loose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely hot' reads as a description of how attractive the organist is, but it is the definition, in the sense of high temperature.
explanation.definitionFit: Weather or an oven described as roasting is uncomfortably warm, an informal intensified way of saying very hot.

clue.text: Send up Fife hooligan princess royal dominated

indicators.note: in a down entry, sending something up makes it read from bottom to top, turning it backwards

blocks.note: ned is Scottish slang for a young hooligan, and Fife is in Scotland
Di, as in Princess Diana
R is the standard abbreviation for royal

explanation.surface: A newspaper story: a Scottish yob mocks the Princess Royal, who was bullied.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Princess royal' looks like the title of Princess Anne, but it splits into two separate pieces. The ned is a Scottish chav.
explanation.definitionFit: Ridden as in guilt-ridden or crime-ridden means overwhelmed or controlled by something, so dominated is a fair past-participle match.

clue.text: Too much on? Felt a pull to travel around America!

indicators.note: travelling around means moving from place to place, so the letters wander into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written for rearranging
A is a standard abbreviation for America

explanation.surface: An overworked person feels a yearning to go off touring the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition comes first with a question mark, because 'too much on' could equally describe clothing or a stage bill.
explanation.definitionFit: Having a full plate is an idiom for being busy with many tasks and responsibilities, so it describes someone overcommitted.

clue.text: In Oz, rabbit and retired horse live by river

indicators.note: retiring means withdrawing or going backwards, so the letters run in the opposite direction

blocks.note: a bay is a reddish-brown horse; retired, it runs backwards
to be is to live or exist
R is the usual abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: An Australian smallholding scene: a rabbit and an old horse living by a river.
explanation.walkthrough: Rabbit is a verb here: in British slang, to rabbit (on) is to chatter endlessly. 'In Oz' says the answer is Australian.
explanation.definitionFit: Yabber is Australian informal speech for talking or chattering, just as rabbiting means talking at length in British slang.

clue.text: Master of arms messing about with toe

indicators.note: messing about means fooling around without order, so the letters get jumbled up

blocks.note: taken as written for rearranging
taken as written for rearranging

explanation.surface: A martial-arts expert playfully fiddling with his toe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Master of arms' reads like a weapons expert as one phrase, but only 'Master' is the definition and 'arms' goes into the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: A maestro is a distinguished expert or virtuoso in some art, especially a conductor, so a master of a craft.

clue.text: Revolutionary prison in low European territory

indicators.note: a revolution turns something right round, so the word is read backwards
one thing placed in another sits between its letters

blocks.note: the can is slang for prison; turned round it reads NAC
to low is to moo, as cattle do

explanation.surface: A rebels' jail set somewhere in the Low Countries.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Low European' suggests the Netherlands, but low is the cow's call. Monaco is a sovereign principality rather than a country in the usual sense, hence territory.
explanation.definitionFit: Monaco is a tiny independent city-state on the Mediterranean coast, a piece of land in Europe ruled by its prince.

clue.text: Acquiring new apartment? That's swell!

indicators.note: acquiring something means taking it in, so one piece ends up held inside another

blocks.note: N is the standard abbreviation for new
a flat is a British apartment
i.e., id est, means 'that is'

explanation.surface: Someone hears a friend is getting a new apartment and cheers that it's great news.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That's swell!' reads as an exclamation of approval, but 'That's' gives IE, which then takes in the new flat; 'swell' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To swell is to grow larger by filling up, as a balloon does when blown up with air, so both are expanding verbs.

clue.text: Nurse with spirit sat on top of express locomotive

indicators.note: the top of a word in a down entry is its opening letter

blocks.note: EN is an enrolled nurse
gin is a spirit
its first letter

explanation.surface: A tipsy nurse rides on the roof of an express train.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'sat on' means placed above, so the first pieces go over the last. EN, an enrolled nurse, is a common crossword abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A locomotive is the powered rail vehicle that pulls a train, and in everyday speech it is simply the train's engine.

clue.text: Aristocrats taking on old, but inexperienced folk

indicators.note: to take on is to take in or absorb, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: nobs is British slang for upper-class people
O is the standard abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: Posh people hiring elderly but untrained staff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking on' suggests employing, but here it means taking the letter inside. Nobs are toffs, British slang for the wealthy upper classes.
explanation.definitionFit: Noob is internet and gaming slang for a newcomer who lacks skill, a beginner still learning the ropes.

clue.text: Criminal beds lad with a thousand rolls of fat

indicators.note: something criminal is wrong or bent, so the letters are twisted out of order

blocks.note: taken as written for rearranging
taken as written
G, a grand, is slang for a thousand

explanation.surface: A crook takes a young man to bed and pays him a thousand pounds, all rather unflattering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Criminal' looks like the subject of the sentence, but it is the signal to rearrange. The definition is singular in form but the answer is a collective term, often used in the plural.
explanation.definitionFit: Saddlebags is informal for deposits of fat on the outer thighs or hips, likened to bags slung over a horse.

clue.text: Bloke making love mostly to make bread

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: a chap is a man
'at it' is a euphemism for having sex; mostly, it loses its last letter

explanation.surface: A man who sleeps with someone mainly to earn money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make bread' looks like slang for earning cash, but bread is the literal definition. 'At it' is British slang for having sex.
explanation.definitionFit: A chapati is a thin, flat, unleavened Indian bread cooked on a griddle, so it is a specific type of loaf.

clue.text: A sad tutor going wild on a road abroad

indicators.note: going wild means losing all control, so the letters scatter into a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written for rearranging
taken as written for rearranging

explanation.surface: A depressed teacher letting rip on a foreign road trip.
explanation.walkthrough: The second 'a' looks like part of 'a road abroad', but it joins the letters to be shuffled, leaving 'road abroad' as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An autostrada is an Italian motorway, a major highway found in a foreign country rather than at home.

clue.text: Tips for narc: experts pull hot rocks on nice tube

indicators.note: the tip of a word is one end of it, and here the leading ends are taken

blocks.clueFragment: narc: experts pull hot rocks on nice
blocks.note: the opening letter of each of these seven words

explanation.surface: An undercover drugs agent gets hints: dealers pass crack around in a smart pipe.
explanation.walkthrough: A narc is American slang for a narcotics officer, and rocks are crack cocaine, so the surface is a drugs bust. A nephron is a kidney tubule.
explanation.definitionFit: A nephron is the tiny tubule in the kidney that filters blood and produces urine, so anatomically it is a tube.

clue.text: Power and sex will be mine!

blocks.note: P is the physics symbol for power
'it' is a euphemism for sex or sex appeal

explanation.surface: A villain's boast that dominance and seduction will soon belong to them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mine' reads as a possessive pronoun in the boast, but it is a noun: a coal mine.
explanation.definitionFit: A pit is a coal mine, especially in Britain, where miners are said to go down the pit to dig coal.

clue.text: Slime having pleasing qualities? Not quite!

indicators.note: not quite means falling just short, so the last letter is removed

blocks.note: having pleasing qualities; not quite complete, it drops its final letter

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether slime has any appeal, and decides it doesn't really.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark and exclamation make it sound like a verdict on slime; 'Not quite' actually trims the word for 'pleasing'.
explanation.definitionFit: Goo is an informal word for any sticky, viscous substance, the same gooey stuff people call slime.

clue.text: Mad at lover? Head to khazi and emit much gas!

indicators.note: something mad is crazy and disordered, so the letters lose their order
the head of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: taken as written for rearranging
its first letter; khazi is British slang for a toilet

explanation.surface: Someone furious with their partner storms off to the loo and breaks wind loudly.
explanation.walkthrough: Khazi is British slang for a lavatory. 'Gas' here means idle chatter, not wind, which is what the toilet scene suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: To gas is informal for chatting idly, so emitting a great deal of it means talking too much, which is to overtalk.

clue.text: Not all call back to get help

indicators.note: not all means only part, so the final letter is removed
going back means travelling the other way, so the letters read right to left

blocks.note: to call someone is to dial them; not all of it loses the last letter

explanation.surface: Advice that you don't have to return every phone call to get assistance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Call back' reads as one phrase, returning a call, but 'call' is the word to trim and 'back' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: Aid is assistance or support given to someone in need, so as nouns the two words are straightforward synonyms.

clue.text: Racy type pulls Her Maj? About time!

indicators.note: about means around, so the earlier pieces wrap round a single letter

blocks.note: to drag is to pull
T is the abbreviation for time
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen's royal cipher; Her Maj is jokey British for Her Majesty

explanation.surface: A saucy character seduces the Queen, and it's high time someone did.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Racy type' suggests someone risqué, but racy here means built for racing; 'pulls' also hints at seduction, but is simply drags.
explanation.definitionFit: A dragster is a car specially built for drag racing, short sprints along a straight strip, so it is a racing vehicle.

clue.text: Cartel bringing in a bit of C4 for bombing

indicators.note: bringing something in means taking it inside, so pieces go into the middle
a bit of a word is a single letter of it, here the first

blocks.note: a ring is a cartel or gang acting together
taken as written
its first character

explanation.surface: A criminal gang smuggling in plastic explosive for a terror attack.
explanation.walkthrough: C4 is a plastic explosive, which makes 'bombing' look like an attack, but it means going very fast.
explanation.definitionFit: Bombing along is informal for travelling at great speed, so it matches racing as a present participle of speeding.

clue.text: Women's stilettos can be instruments of torture

blocks.note: W is the abbreviation for women, as on a toilet door
stilettos are high heels

explanation.surface: A wry complaint that women's spiky high heels are agony to wear.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites agreement that heels hurt; the definition is literal, a historical device on which victims were broken.
explanation.definitionFit: The breaking wheel was a medieval execution device, with victims tied to it and their limbs smashed, so wheels were torture tools.

clue.text: Excitement as Raoul spun out

indicators.note: spinning out of control sends things flying in every direction, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written for rearranging

explanation.surface: Thrills as a man called Raoul loses control, perhaps in a racing car.
explanation.walkthrough: Raoul looks like a person, but his name is simply letters to rearrange together with 'as'.
explanation.definitionFit: Arousal is a state of heightened stimulation or excitement, whether emotional, physical or sexual, so the nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: Criminal exposed by Parisian article on wife

blocks.note: out means revealed or exposed
la is a French word for 'the'
W is the abbreviation for wife

explanation.surface: A crook unmasked by a French newspaper's story about his wife.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' means placed above, so the article sits over the wife. 'Article' suggests a newspaper piece, but it is the grammatical article.
explanation.definitionFit: An outlaw is a fugitive or lawbreaker, someone who lives outside the law, so both describe a person who commits crimes.

clue.text: Gold soldiers stashed in empty Liverpool plant

indicators.note: something stashed in a place is hidden inside it, so these pieces go in the middle
emptying a word removes its insides, leaving just the two outer letters

blocks.note: its first and last letters
Au is the chemical symbol for gold
RE is the Royal Engineers, a British army corps

explanation.surface: Stolen gold, hidden by troops inside a deserted Liverpool factory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' suggests an industrial site in the Liverpool scene, but it is the botanical sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The laurel is an evergreen shrub, the bay tree, whose leaves were woven into wreaths for victors, so it is a plant.

clue.text: In hearing, launderer's confession is nonsense

indicators.note: in hearing means as it reaches the ear, so the spoken form counts, not the spelling

blocks.note: what someone who does laundry would admit to

explanation.surface: At a court hearing, a money launderer's admission is dismissed as rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hearing' and 'launderer' suggest a court case about dirty money; the launderer just washes clothes, and the confession is spoken.
explanation.definitionFit: Eyewash is informal for talk intended to deceive or impress, insincere rubbish, much like hogwash or claptrap.

clue.text: Obstruct prurient fools heading for threesome

indicators.note: to fool about is to play around, so the letters are mucked about into new positions
the heading of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: taken as written for rearranging
its first letter

explanation.surface: Lustful idiots barge in, set on a threesome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fools' looks like a plural noun that 'prurient' describes, but it is a verb meaning plays about with the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To interrupt a process or flow is to break in and hinder it, so it can mean to block or impede, like obstruct.

clue.text: A way to stop our man getting speed

indicators.note: a stopper plugs a gap, so one piece is pushed inside another to block it

blocks.note: he is the pronoun for a man
taken as written
St is the abbreviation for street, a way

explanation.surface: A spy-story plan to halt our agent before he picks up pace.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like a chase scene; 'A way' supplies two pieces that go inside the pronoun.
explanation.definitionFit: Haste is swiftness of movement or action, hurrying, so as nouns both mean quickness in doing something.

clue.text: Climber stuck on top of Everest might have this

definitions.text: Climber stuck on top of Everest might have this

indicators.note: the top of a word in a down entry is its first letter

blocks.note: the hop is a climbing plant grown up poles for beer
its first letter

explanation.surface: A mountaineer stranded at the summit of Everest clings to optimism.
explanation.walkthrough: As a whole the clue describes the feeling of a stranded mountaineer; within the wordplay the climber is a plant, not a person.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone stranded on a high summit can only wish and trust that rescue will come, so optimism is all they have left.

clue.text: Worthy old relative drugs grasping duke

indicators.note: grasping means holding tight, so one piece is held between others

blocks.note: a gran is a grandmother
E is ecstasy, so two of them make drugs
D is the abbreviation for duke

explanation.surface: A respectable elderly relative is busted for drugging a duke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worthy' looks like an adjective describing the relative, but it is a noun. The relative and the drugs together hold the duke between them.
explanation.definitionFit: A worthy, as a noun, is a notable or esteemed person, and a grandee is likewise someone of high rank and influence.

clue.text: Catty drinkers knocked back Bud with a soprano

indicators.note: knocking something back sends it backwards, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: bud is a buddy or pal; knocked back it reads in reverse
per means 'a', as in fifty miles per hour
S is the abbreviation for soprano

explanation.surface: Bitchy drinkers down Budweiser alongside a singer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knocked back' and 'Bud' suggest downing a beer, but Bud is a friend. 'Catty' means cat-like, not spiteful.
explanation.definitionFit: Cats drink by scooping liquid with the tongue, so feline animals at a water bowl are creatures that lap it up.
